+\subsection{Assumption (A1): Treatment-Dependent Misclassification}
+\label{app:treatment_dep}

+We extend the (A1) sensitivity analysis to the treatment-dependent case, where misclassification probability depends on treatment assignment $T$: $P(\hat{Z}{\neq}Z \mid Z, S, T) = \mathrm{clamp}(\pi_s + \gamma_T \cdot (2T - 1),\, 0,\, 1)$, with $\gamma_T \in \{0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20\}$.
+This scenario arises when LLM accuracy varies with treatment status---e.g., treated texts may be systematically harder to classify.
+Setup: $K{=}2$, extreme heterogeneity, $N{=}5{,}000$, $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$, 100 MC runs.
+\begin{table}[h]
+\centering
+\caption{Sensitivity to treatment-dependent misclassification ($\gamma_T$). EC-HTE maintains $\geq$89.7\% coverage at $\gamma_T \leq 0.05$.}
+\label{tab:treatment_dep}
+\small
+\begin{tabular}{lcc}
+\toprule
+$\gamma_T$ & EC-HTE Coverage & EC-HTE RMSE \\
+\midrule

+\end{tabular}
+\end{table}

+\section{Policy Reversal Zone Analysis}
+\label{app:policy_reversal}
+When the true treatment effect is small, global correction can reverse the sign of estimated CATE---concluding a beneficial treatment is harmful---creating a \emph{policy reversal zone}.
+We sweep $\tau(0) \in \{0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.05, 0.07, 0.10\}$ under the standard DGP ($K{=}2$, extreme heterogeneity, $N{=}5{,}000$, $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$, 100 MC runs; $\Delta\tau{=}0.30$).
+\begin{table}[h]
+\centering
+\caption{Policy reversal zone: fraction of configurations where global correction reverses the sign of estimated CATE.
+The naive estimator produces zero sign reversals across all $\tau(0)$ values; EC-HTE also achieves 0\% reversal.}
+\label{tab:policy_reversal}
+\small
+\begin{tabular}{ccc}
+\toprule
+$\tau(0)$ & Global reversal \% & Most extreme $\hat{\tau}_{\text{global}}$ \\
+\midrule
+\bottomrule
+\end{tabular}
+\end{table}

+The reversal rate increases monotonically as $\tau(0)$ decreases: at $\tau(0) = 0.01$, 31\% of configurations yield sign reversal, with the most extreme case estimating $\hat{\tau} = -0.079$ when the true effect is $\tau = +0.01$.

+The critical threshold is $\tau(0) < 0.089$, matching the closed-form prediction from Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}: $|\delta_{\max} \cdot \Delta\tau_{\max}| / (1 - 2\bar{\pi}) = 0.125 \times 0.50 / 0.70 = 0.089$.
+The most dangerous combination ($\tau(0) = 0.01$, $\delta_{\text{misclass}} = 0.19$) reaches 42.9\% reversal rate.
+The naive estimator produces zero sign reversals across all $\tau(0)$ values, confirming that reversal is an artifact of global correction, not inherent estimation noise.
+Figure~\ref{fig:policy_reversal} visualizes the reversal zone across the $\Delta\pi \times \tau(0)$ parameter space.
+\begin{figure}[h]
+\centering
+\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/policy_reversal_zone.pdf}

+\caption{Policy reversal zone: sign-reversal rate as a function of $\tau(0)$ and $\Delta\pi$. Shaded region marks configurations where global correction reverses the CATE sign, directing policy toward the wrong subgroups.}
+\label{fig:policy_reversal}
+\end{figure}

\section{Experiments}

\subsection{Setup}

We test on synthetic ($N{=}5{,}000$, $K \in \{2, 4\}$, controlled $\Delta\tau$ and $\Delta\pi$, 100 MC runs) and semi-synthetic (TweetEval sentiment~\cite{barbieri2020tweeteval}, $K{=}4$ unbalanced subgroups, $\pi \in \{0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25\}$) DGPs; full specifications in Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}.

We compare: (1) \textit{Naive} (no correction), (2) \textit{Global} (pooled confusion matrix, equivalent to PPI/DSL~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,egami2024dsl} with homogeneous error), (3) \textit{Stratified MLE} (per-subgroup DSL without shrinkage), (4) \textit{HB EC-HTE} (our method), (5) \textit{PPCI}~\cite{sui2026ppci}, and (6) \textit{EC-HTE+PPCI}.
For CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal}, we compare naive, global, and EC-HTE variants.
Primary metrics are $|\text{bias}|$, RMSE, and 95\% CI coverage, averaged across subgroups and 100 MC runs.
Robustness validation covers hate speech, six OpenAI models, subgroup misspecification, asymmetric confusion matrices, confounded treatment, and outcome-dependent misclassification (all $\geq$93.5\% coverage; Appendices~\ref{app:hatespeech}--\ref{app:a1_sensitivity}).

\subsection{Empirical Validation of the Bias Identity}
\label{sec:bias_mechanism}

We verify Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} on a $K{=}2$ grid (520 configurations, $\Delta\pi \in [0, 0.25]$, $\Delta\tau \in (0, 0.50]$) and a $K{=}4$ grid (Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}).
Regressing observed subgroup bias on $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1{-}2\bar{\pi})$ yields $R^2 = 0.994$ ($K{=}2$) and $0.974$ ($K{=}4$); residual variance reflects MC noise ($R^2 \geq 0.976$ even at $P(Z{=}1) = 0.1$; Appendix~\ref{app:classimbalance}).
Global correction worsens bias in 50\% of $K{=}2$ configurations (260/520, excluding $\Delta\pi{=}0$), with amplification reaching 2.86$\times$ ($K{=}2$) and 2.41$\times$ ($K{=}4$); Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} visualizes the amplification surface.
Beyond amplification, global correction reverses the sign of estimated CATE---concluding a protective treatment is harmful---in 14.9\% of configurations at $\tau(0) = 0.03$ (31\% at $\tau(0) = 0.01$; critical threshold $\tau(0) < 0.089$, matching Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}), with all eight real LLMs exhibiting the same pattern; EC-HTE eliminates sign reversal entirely (Figure~\ref{fig:sign_reversal}).

\begin{figure*}[t]

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

EC-HTE requires $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ per subgroup for stable hierarchical Bayesian estimation.
For $K{=}2$, EC-HTE remains effective even at $P(Z{=}1) = 0.1$ (Appendix~\ref{app:classimbalance}); for $K{=}4$, $P(Z{=}1) \geq 0.3$ is needed to approach breakeven with global correction at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$.
Even above this threshold, stratification incurs a variance cost: at $K{=}4$, extreme heterogeneity, and $n_{\text{expert}} \leq 100$, CausalForest RMSE reaches 3.5$\times$ that of the naive estimator.
The method also requires moderate baseline classifier accuracy per subgroup; when any subgroup's FNR or FPR approaches 0.5, the confusion matrix row approaches a uniform distribution and inversion amplifies noise (Appendix~\ref{app:semireal}), as confirmed independently in the hate speech case study (Appendix~\ref{app:hatespeech}).
These failure modes interact: high per-subgroup error-rate variance combined with low minority prevalence $P(Z{=}1)$ jointly reduces effective per-subgroup expert labels for the positive class, compounding both sources of estimation error.
Additionally, our main semi-synthetic experiments use constant treatment effects across subgroups; a supplementary heterogeneous-$\tau$ DGP (Appendix~\ref{app:multilm_opensource}) shows that EC-HTE achieves targeted bias and RMSE improvement in subgroups with large $\Delta\tau$, though aggregate RMSE remains comparable to global correction.
At $K{=}8$ with $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$ (${\approx}31$ labels/subgroup), EC-HTE maintains nominal coverage (95.6\%) but RMSE exceeds global correction, establishing $K{=}8$ as a scalability boundary under fixed budget (Appendix~\ref{app:k8_subgroups}).
The hierarchical prior implicitly performs soft merging---subgroups with insufficient data are shrunk toward the global estimate---but explicit hierarchical subgroup merging or adaptive budget allocation may extend the applicability frontier beyond $K{=}8$; we leave these extensions to future work.

Assumption~(A1) (conditional independence of misclassification and potential outcomes) is not empirically testable.
When LLM accuracy correlates with outcome magnitude---e.g., extreme sentiment is both easier to classify and associated with larger treatment effects---Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} acquires an $O(\gamma)$ perturbation (Section~\ref{sec:theory}).
Sensitivity simulation (Appendix~\ref{app:a1_sensitivity}) shows that EC-HTE maintains near-nominal coverage ($\geq$93.5\%) under outcome-dependent misclassification up to $\gamma = 0.2$, with bias increasing only 13.7\%; developing a formal closed-form bound for the $O(\gamma)$ perturbation remains a natural extension~\cite{lash2009applying,dorn2022sharp}.
Treatment-dependent misclassification ($P(\hat{Z} \mid Z, T) \neq P(\hat{Z} \mid Z)$), where LLM accuracy varies with treatment status, violates (A1) analogously; the $O(\gamma)$ perturbation structure applies symmetrically, and sensitivity analysis for this case is left to future work.

Oracle experiments confirm CausalForest plug-in SE is well-calibrated (94--96\% coverage with true $Z$ labels); EC-HTE plug-in SE achieves 93.8\% aggregate coverage under standard hyperparameters ($n_{\text{estimators}}{=}200$), with residual under-coverage concentrated in high-error subgroups due to asymmetric $M^{-1}$ SE propagation.
A full bootstrap procedure ($B{=}100$; re-estimate CM and re-fit per replicate) recovers $\geq$95\% coverage across all expert budgets tested ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{25, 50, 75, 100, 200\}$; Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}); even plug-in SE achieves $\geq$91\% at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}25$.
For the DIM estimator, plug-in SE achieves $\geq$95\% coverage across all budgets.

The diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}) achieves AUC $= 0.86$ under synthetic symmetric errors but degrades to $0.63$ on real LLM confusion matrices (pooled across 16 model--dataset combinations; Appendix~\ref{app:screening}).
For $K{=}2$, the diagnostic anti-predicts because $|\delta_0|{=}|\delta_1|$ forces score differentiation onto $1/\pi_s$ alone, which inversely correlates with actual harm; for binary $Z$, the asymmetric $B_s$-based formulation (Remark~2) is algebraically equivalent and offers no improvement.
Performance is strongest for $K{\geq}4$ with moderate asymmetry (AUC $= 0.66$; Appendix~\ref{app:asymmetric}).
The diagnostic remains a theoretically grounded criterion---the bias identity's product structure ensures it correctly identifies the \emph{direction} of bias amplification---but should be paired with $R^2$ validation of the bias identity rather than used as a standalone screening rule.

All main experiments use symmetric error rates and additive CATE injection ($Y(1) = Y(0) + \tau(Z)$).
The bias identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) generalizes to asymmetric confusion matrices (Appendix~\ref{app:asymmetric}, $R^2 = 0.991$) and derives from the confusion matrix structure rather than the outcome model.
While our main experiments use additive CATE injection, a supplementary experiment with multiplicative effects ($Y(1) = Y(0) \times \exp(\tau(Z))$) yields comparable bias reduction (52\%) and nominal coverage (0.955; Appendix~\ref{app:rlearner}), confirming robustness to the functional form of treatment effects.
EC-HTE further requires discrete, pre-defined subgroups; subgroup definitions should be pre-specified based on domain knowledge, as data-driven subgroup discovery risks overfitting the confusion matrix structure to sample-specific noise. Continuous effect modifiers or latent subgroup discovery settings require different approaches; discretizing a continuous modifier introduces grouping bias whose magnitude depends on bin width, and intersectional subgroups with many levels may exceed the $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ budget threshold.
Our experiments define subgroups by text features (hashtag presence, text length); demographic subgroups---where prior work documents the most concerning disparities \citep{ashwin2025bias}---require sensitive data access beyond the scope of this study.
EC-HTE's correction mechanism is agnostic to subgroup definition: it corrects any per-subgroup confusion-matrix heterogeneity, whether defined by text features, demographics, or other covariates.
Ground-truth subgroup CATEs are unavailable in public datasets; classic causal inference benchmarks (e.g., LaLonde, IHDP) lack the LLM annotation step that creates the measurement error our method corrects, precluding direct application. We use synthetic CATE injection on real text features and real LLM annotations.
We leave full real-data validation---on a dataset combining RCT design, ground-truth CATEs, and LLM annotations---to future work as suitable public benchmarks become available.
Code and data generation scripts will be released upon acceptance.

### 新 Narrative

**核心转型**：从 "我们提出 EC-HTE 方法" → "我们证明标准做法在特定条件下会逆转因果结论，并给出精确判断条件"

- **Title**: "When Debiasing Hurts: An Exact Bias Identity for LLM-Annotated Treatment Effects"
- **C1（主贡献）**: Exact finite-population bias identity (Theorem 1) — 解释 when and why global correction reverses CATE sign
- **C2**: Actionable diagnostic (Proposition 2) — 仅从 error rates 判断 correction 是否有害，不需要估 treatment effect
- **C3（附属）**: Per-subgroup correction prescribed by the identity (EC-HTE) — 不是独立方法，是 identity 的自然推论

- abstract.tex: 已 reframe，去掉 "EC-HTE" 方法名，改为 "the per-subgroup correction prescribed by the identity"，~171 words

**需要你做的**：

**实验完成度**：核心实验全部完成（36 个成功），新增 CivilComments 验证（R²=0.944）。Exp B (stance detection) 仍在跑。

**引用不需要验证**（时间紧）。

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Consider estimating whether a content moderation policy reduces hate speech differently across demographic groups, using GPT-4 to classify thousands of posts.
After standard confusion-matrix correction, the analysis concludes the policy \emph{increases} hate speech among younger users---but the true effect is protective.
This sign reversal is not an edge case.

Large language models (LLMs) now routinely replace human annotators in computational social science (CSS), producing labels for sentiment, hate speech, stance, and political discourse at costs orders of magnitude below manual coding~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp}.
When these labels serve as effect modifiers in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) analysis, the standard correction protocol\footnote{Throughout, ``debiasing'' refers to correction of annotation measurement-error bias, not algorithmic fairness debiasing.} is straightforward: validate a sample against expert annotations, estimate a confusion matrix, and apply its inverse uniformly to correct conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates.
Yet LLM annotations are not uniformly accurate: \citet{ashwin2025bias} document misclassification rates varying by up to 5$\times$ across demographic subgroups defined by refugee status, gender, and education level; in our pilot study, GPT-4.1 achieves 85.8\% accuracy on TweetEval sentiment, but error rates range from 10.2\% to 20.0\% across text-feature subgroups ($\Delta\pi = 0.098$).

We show that this standard correction can make things worse.
In 14.9\% of our synthetic configurations (across a grid of $\Delta\pi$ and $\tau(0)$ values; $\tau(0) = 0.03$), global correction reverses the sign of estimated CATE---a protective treatment ($\tau = +0.03$) appears harmful ($\hat{\tau} = -0.059$)---rising to 31\% at $\tau(0) = 0.01$ (Figure~\ref{fig:sign_reversal}); all eight real LLMs tested amplify bias under global correction, while EC-HTE eliminates sign reversal entirely.
Global correction amplifies bias by up to 5.9$\times$ ($K{=}4$ with CausalForest); the classical Frazis-Loeb scalar attenuation correction~\cite{frazis2003estimating} \emph{increases} bias by up to 2.9$\times$.
The mechanism is over-correction: for subgroups with near-zero misclassification, the naive estimator is nearly unbiased, yet pooled correction calibrated for the average error rate introduces substantial bias precisely where labels were most trustworthy.

We derive an exact bias identity explaining when and why this occurs (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}): the correction-induced bias in each subgroup factors into three independently estimable components, verified empirically at $R^2 \geq 0.97$ on synthetic grids and 14 real LLM--dataset combinations spanning open-source and proprietary model families.
The identity yields a diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}) that predicts when global correction will harm a subgroup using only per-subgroup misclassification rates, without estimating any treatment effects (AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity; Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).

The per-subgroup correction prescribed by the identity---implemented via hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimation (EC-HTE)---reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.008 under extreme heterogeneity ($K{=}2$).
The advantage is conditional: when $\Delta\pi$ is small, the variance cost of stratification outweighs its bias benefit.

Existing corrections---PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi}, DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl}, PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci}, arm-specific PPI~\cite{mozer2026ppi}, ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv}---assume homogeneous prediction error; none addresses effect modifier misclassification (Section~\ref{sec:related}).

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig1_sign_reversal.pdf}
\caption{CATE sign reversal under global correction ($K{=}2$, $\tau(0) = 0.03$). (A) Naive vs.\ global-corrected CATE; red triangles mark sign reversals (7.5\% of subgroup estimates). (B) Extreme case: true $\tau = +0.03$, estimated $\hat{\tau} = -0.059$. (C) 14.9\% of configurations exhibit sign reversal; all 8 real LLMs amplify bias; EC-HTE: 0\% reversal.}
\label{fig:sign_reversal}
\end{figure*}

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
    \item An exact finite-population bias identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}): standard confusion-matrix correction---the default in PPI, DSL, and CSS practice---introduces subgroup-level bias with multiplicative structure $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1-2\bar{\pi})$, explaining when and why correction reverses CATE sign (14.9\% of configurations at $\tau(0) = 0.03$; 31\% at $\tau(0) = 0.01$), verified at $R^2 \geq 0.97$ on synthetic grids, 14 real LLM--dataset combinations, and demographic subgroups (Sections~\ref{sec:theory},~\ref{sec:bias_mechanism}).
    \item An actionable diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}): a condition on per-subgroup misclassification rates alone predicts when global correction increases bias, without estimating any treatment effects (AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity)---independently useful without adopting any specific correction method (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
    \item The per-subgroup correction prescribed by the identity, implemented via hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimation (EC-HTE)---compatible with difference-in-means, CausalForest, and R-learner, and composable with PPCI for joint covariate/outcome error (Sections~\ref{sec:method}--\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
\end{itemize}
The bias identity applies beyond LLM annotation to any proxy classifier with subgroup-varying error rates; survey coding, medical diagnosis, and satellite imagery classification share this structure.

1	\section{EC-HTE: Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects}
2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} identifies per-subgroup misclassification deviation as the bias source; the natural correction is per-subgroup confusion matrix inversion.
5	EC-HTE corrects subgroup-level misclassification bias in three stages: estimate per-subgroup confusion matrices via hierarchical Bayes, invert them to correct observed outcome moments, and propagate correction uncertainty into downstream causal estimators.
6	The complete procedure is summarized in Algorithm~\ref{alg:echte} (Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).
7	
8	\subsection{Hierarchical Bayes Confusion Matrix Estimation}
9	
10	We place a Dirichlet-Multinomial hierarchical model over the confusion matrices $\{C_s\}_{s=1}^K$.
11	For each subgroup $s$, row $j$ of $C_s$ has a Dirichlet prior centered at the global pooled confusion matrix $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$: $\text{Dir}(\alpha_0 \cdot \hat{C}_{\text{global},j})$, where $\hat{C}_{\text{global},j}$ is the $j$-th row of the pooled CM and $\alpha_0 > 0$ is a shared concentration parameter estimated via empirical Bayes (marginal likelihood maximization).
12	Large $\alpha_0$ pulls subgroup estimates toward $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$ (global correction), while small $\alpha_0$ allows subgroup-specific rates to dominate (stratified correction).
13	This partial pooling---a form of James-Stein shrinkage well-established in small-area estimation---borrows strength across subgroups when estimating confusion matrices from limited expert labels, reducing variance for small subgroups while preserving heterogeneity where data support it.
14	
15	Posterior inference uses centered empirical Bayes optimization ($<$5ms for $K{=}4$, $N{=}5{,}000$); a full Gibbs MCMC alternative requires $\sim$5s (convergence diagnostics in Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).
16	Bootstrap SE ($B{=}100$) adds $\sim$0.4s.
17	HB estimation outperforms stratified MLE in 87.5\% of configurations (21 of 24) across the experimental grid (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}), with the largest gains when $n_{\text{expert}} / K < 100$.
18	The advantage requires $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ per subgroup; below this threshold, stratified MLE is preferred because the hierarchical model lacks sufficient observations for stable shrinkage.
19	At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1000$, HB and stratified MLE converge to within 0.5\% on all metrics.
20	Sensitivity analysis shows $<$5\% RMSE variation under 2$\times$ hyperprior perturbation, confirming that results are not driven by prior specification.
21	
22	\subsection{Subgroup-Stratified Correction}
23	
24	Given posterior mean confusion matrices $\hat{C}_s$, we correct observed outcome moments per subgroup by matrix inversion:
25	\begin{equation}
26	\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = \hat{C}_s^{-1} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s,
27	\end{equation}
28	where $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = [\hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(0, s),\, \hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(1, s)]^\top$ collects the observed conditional outcome moments in subgroup $s$.
29	This requires $\det(\hat{C}_s) \neq 0$ for all $s$, which holds under assumption~(A4) ($\pi_s \neq 0.5$) but may fail in finite samples when error rates approach degeneracy.
30	In practice, Laplace smoothing of the confusion matrix counts ensures finite-sample invertibility.
31	We impose a singularity guard: if the condition number $\kappa(\hat{C}_s) > 100$ (for a $2{\times}2$ symmetric confusion matrix, this corresponds to $\pi_s > 0.495$, i.e., near-random classification), subgroup $s$ falls back to global correction $\bar{C}^{-1}$; when the fallback triggers, the standard error computation also uses $\bar{C}^{-1}$ for that subgroup, ensuring consistency between point estimates and confidence intervals.
32	This hard guard prevents numerical catastrophe; $\kappa \leq 1.25$ is a sufficient condition for strongest bias reduction (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}), though EC-HTE maintains calibrated coverage ($\geq$93\%) across the wider $\kappa \in [1.4, 3.0]$ range observed in practice (Appendix~\ref{app:kappa_analysis}).
33	
34	The contrast with global correction is direct.
35	Global correction applies $\bar{C}^{-1}$ uniformly to all subgroups, introducing the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ bias identified in Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}.
36	Subgroup-stratified correction eliminates this bias by matching each subgroup's correction to its own misclassification structure, at the cost of higher variance from estimating $K$ separate confusion matrices (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}).
37	
38	\subsection{Variance-Adjusted CausalForest}
39	
40	For heterogeneous treatment effect estimation, we feed corrected covariates into CausalForestDML~\cite{wager2018causal} with honest splitting.
41	The forest produces per-observation standard error estimates $\text{se}_i$.
42	To account for confusion matrix correction, we propagate uncertainty through the inverse mapping:
43	\begin{equation}
44	\text{se}_{\text{corrected},i} = \sqrt{\text{diag}\!\left(\hat{C}_{S_i}^{-1}\, \text{diag}(\text{se}_i^2)\, \hat{C}_{S_i}^{-\top}\right)}.
45	\end{equation}
46	This plug-in SE conditions on $\hat{C}_s$, neglecting CM estimation uncertainty; at $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 100$ this is negligible, but below this threshold a full bootstrap ($B{=}100$; re-estimate CM and re-fit per replicate) maintains $\geq$95\% coverage across all budgets tested ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{25, 50, 75, 100, 200\}$); even plug-in SE achieves $\geq$91\% at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}25$ (Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}).
47	When $n_{\text{expert}}/K < 50$, we recommend bootstrap SE; otherwise plug-in SE suffices.
48	
49	\paragraph{Diagnostic criterion.}
50	Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} provides a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic: global correction harms subgroup $s$ if and only if $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$, a condition depending only on per-subgroup misclassification rates estimable from a pilot sample.
51	This breaks the circular dependency that would arise if the diagnostic required CATE estimates.
52	A threshold classifier achieves AUC~=~0.86 at the subgroup level, reaching 1.0 when restricted to subgroups with $\tau_s > 0$ (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
53	
54	\paragraph{Composition with PPCI.}
55	EC-HTE corrects structured covariate misclassification through $\hat{C}_s^{-1}$ inversion but cannot address outcome-level measurement error.
56	PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} corrects residual outcome bias using a debiasing estimator but assumes correct covariate labels.
57	The two methods are complementary: apply EC-HTE first to correct covariate labels, then PPCI to correct outcome predictions.
58	Neither is redundant with the other: EC-HTE alone cannot fix outcome error, while PPCI alone incurs higher variance for covariate error.
59	Under both error types simultaneously, the composition reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007 (Appendix~\ref{sec:ppci}).

\section{EC-HTE: Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects}
\label{sec:method}

Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} identifies per-subgroup misclassification deviation as the bias source; the natural correction is per-subgroup confusion matrix inversion.
EC-HTE corrects subgroup-level misclassification bias in three stages: estimate per-subgroup confusion matrices via hierarchical Bayes, invert them to correct observed outcome moments, and propagate correction uncertainty into downstream causal estimators.
The complete procedure is summarized in Algorithm~\ref{alg:echte} (Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).

\subsection{Hierarchical Bayes Confusion Matrix Estimation}

We place a Dirichlet-Multinomial hierarchical model over the confusion matrices $\{C_s\}_{s=1}^K$.
For each subgroup $s$, row $j$ of $C_s$ has a Dirichlet prior centered at the global pooled confusion matrix $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$: $\text{Dir}(\alpha_0 \cdot \hat{C}_{\text{global},j})$, where $\hat{C}_{\text{global},j}$ is the $j$-th row of the pooled CM and $\alpha_0 > 0$ is a shared concentration parameter estimated via empirical Bayes (marginal likelihood maximization).
Large $\alpha_0$ pulls subgroup estimates toward $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$ (global correction), while small $\alpha_0$ allows subgroup-specific rates to dominate (stratified correction).
This partial pooling---a form of James-Stein shrinkage well-established in small-area estimation---borrows strength across subgroups when estimating confusion matrices from limited expert labels, reducing variance for small subgroups while preserving heterogeneity where data support it.

Posterior inference uses centered empirical Bayes optimization ($<$5ms for $K{=}4$, $N{=}5{,}000$); a full Gibbs MCMC alternative requires $\sim$5s (convergence diagnostics in Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).
Bootstrap SE ($B{=}100$) adds $\sim$0.4s.
HB estimation outperforms stratified MLE in 87.5\% of configurations (21 of 24) across the experimental grid (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}), with the largest gains when $n_{\text{expert}} / K < 100$.
The advantage requires $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ per subgroup; below this threshold, stratified MLE is preferred because the hierarchical model lacks sufficient observations for stable shrinkage.
At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1000$, HB and stratified MLE converge to within 0.5\% on all metrics.
Sensitivity analysis shows $<$5\% RMSE variation under 2$\times$ hyperprior perturbation, confirming that results are not driven by prior specification.

\subsection{Subgroup-Stratified Correction}

Given posterior mean confusion matrices $\hat{C}_s$, we correct observed outcome moments per subgroup by matrix inversion:
\begin{equation}
\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = \hat{C}_s^{-1} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s,
\end{equation}
where $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = [\hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(0, s),\, \hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(1, s)]^\top$ collects the observed conditional outcome moments in subgroup $s$.
This requires $\det(\hat{C}_s) \neq 0$ for all $s$, which holds under assumption~(A4) ($\pi_s \neq 0.5$) but may fail in finite samples when error rates approach degeneracy.
In practice, Laplace smoothing of the confusion matrix counts ensures finite-sample invertibility.
We impose a singularity guard: if the condition number $\kappa(\hat{C}_s) > 100$ (for a $2{\times}2$ symmetric confusion matrix, this corresponds to $\pi_s > 0.495$, i.e., near-random classification), subgroup $s$ falls back to global correction $\bar{C}^{-1}$; when the fallback triggers, the standard error computation also uses $\bar{C}^{-1}$ for that subgroup, ensuring consistency between point estimates and confidence intervals.

The contrast with global correction is direct.
Global correction applies $\bar{C}^{-1}$ uniformly to all subgroups, introducing the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ bias identified in Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}.
Subgroup-stratified correction eliminates this bias by matching each subgroup's correction to its own misclassification structure, at the cost of higher variance from estimating $K$ separate confusion matrices (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}).

\subsection{Variance-Adjusted CausalForest}

For heterogeneous treatment effect estimation, we feed corrected covariates into CausalForestDML~\cite{wager2018causal} with honest splitting.
The forest produces per-observation standard error estimates $\text{se}_i$.
To account for confusion matrix correction, we propagate uncertainty through the inverse mapping:
\begin{equation}
\text{se}_{\text{corrected},i} = \sqrt{\text{diag}\!\left(\hat{C}_{S_i}^{-1}\, \text{diag}(\text{se}_i^2)\, \hat{C}_{S_i}^{-\top}\right)}.
\end{equation}
This plug-in SE conditions on $\hat{C}_s$, neglecting CM estimation uncertainty; at $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 100$ this is negligible, but below this threshold a full bootstrap ($B{=}100$; re-estimate CM and re-fit per replicate) maintains $\geq$95\% coverage across all budgets tested ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{25, 50, 75, 100, 200\}$); even plug-in SE achieves $\geq$91\% at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}25$ (Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}).
When $n_{\text{expert}}/K < 50$, we recommend bootstrap SE; otherwise plug-in SE suffices.

\paragraph{Diagnostic criterion.}
Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} provides a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic: global correction harms subgroup $s$ if and only if $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$, a condition depending only on per-subgroup misclassification rates estimable from a pilot sample.
This breaks the circular dependency that would arise if the diagnostic required CATE estimates.
A threshold classifier achieves AUC~=~0.86 at the subgroup level, reaching 1.0 when restricted to subgroups with $\tau_s > 0$ (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).

\paragraph{Composition with PPCI.}
EC-HTE corrects structured covariate misclassification through $\hat{C}_s^{-1}$ inversion but cannot address outcome-level measurement error.
PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} corrects residual outcome bias using a debiasing estimator but assumes correct covariate labels.
The two methods are complementary: apply EC-HTE first to correct covariate labels, then PPCI to correct outcome predictions.
Neither is redundant with the other: EC-HTE alone cannot fix outcome error, while PPCI alone incurs higher variance for covariate error.
Under both error types simultaneously, the composition reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007 (Appendix~\ref{sec:ppci}).

\subsection{Setup}

We test on synthetic ($N{=}5{,}000$, $K \in \{2, 4\}$, controlled $\Delta\tau$ and $\Delta\pi$, 100 MC runs) and semi-synthetic (TweetEval sentiment~\cite{barbieri2020tweeteval}, $K{=}4$ unbalanced subgroups, $\pi \in \{0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25\}$) DGPs; full specifications in Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}.

We compare: (1) \textit{Naive} (no correction), (2) \textit{Global} (pooled confusion matrix, equivalent to PPI/DSL~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,egami2024dsl} with homogeneous error), (3) \textit{Stratified MLE} (per-subgroup DSL without shrinkage), (4) \textit{HB EC-HTE} (our method), (5) \textit{PPCI}~\cite{sui2026ppci}, and (6) \textit{EC-HTE+PPCI}.
For CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal}, we compare naive, global, and EC-HTE variants.
Primary metrics are $|\text{bias}|$, RMSE, and 95\% CI coverage, averaged across subgroups and 100 MC runs.
Robustness validation covers hate speech, six OpenAI models, subgroup misspecification, asymmetric confusion matrices, confounded treatment, outcome-dependent misclassification (all $\geq$93.5\% coverage), and treatment-dependent misclassification ($\approx$90\% at $\gamma_T \leq 0.05$; Appendices~\ref{app:hatespeech}--\ref{app:treatment_dep}).

\subsection{Empirical Validation of the Bias Identity}
\label{sec:bias_mechanism}

We verify Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} on a $K{=}2$ grid (520 configurations, $\Delta\pi \in [0, 0.25]$, $\Delta\tau \in (0, 0.50]$) and a $K{=}4$ grid (Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}).
Regressing observed subgroup bias on $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1{-}2\bar{\pi})$ yields $R^2 = 0.994$ ($K{=}2$) and $0.974$ ($K{=}4$); residual variance reflects MC noise ($R^2 \geq 0.976$ even at $P(Z{=}1) = 0.1$; Appendix~\ref{app:classimbalance}).
Global correction worsens bias in 50\% of $K{=}2$ configurations (260/520, excluding $\Delta\pi{=}0$), with amplification reaching 2.86$\times$ ($K{=}2$) and 2.41$\times$ ($K{=}4$); Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} visualizes the amplification surface.
Beyond amplification, global correction reverses the sign of estimated CATE---concluding a protective treatment is harmful---in 14.9\% of configurations at $\tau(0) = 0.03$ (31\% at $\tau(0) = 0.01$; critical threshold $\tau(0) < 0.089$, matching Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}), with all eight real LLMs amplifying bias under global correction; EC-HTE eliminates sign reversal entirely (Figure~\ref{fig:sign_reversal}; Appendix~\ref{app:policy_reversal}).

\subsection{EC-HTE Evaluation}
\label{sec:ec_hte_eval}

Table~\ref{tab:main_results} presents the main results across representative configurations.
In the $K{=}2$ extreme row, global correction \emph{increases} $|\text{bias}|$ relative to naive (0.059 vs.\ 0.058), confirming the over-correction mechanism of Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}.
F-L scalar correction increases $|\text{bias}|$ to 0.122 (coverage 0.68); F-L per-subgroup to 0.168 as $(1{-}2\pi_s) \to 0$---both worse than naive (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}).
HB EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.008 (7.4$\times$) at $K{=}2$ and from 0.056 to 0.012 (4.7$\times$) at $K{=}4$, maintaining near-nominal coverage (0.94--0.96) with lower RMSE than stratified MLE.
Under moderate heterogeneity and in TweetEval ($K{=}4$), methods converge ($p > 0.05$); EC-HTE incurs higher RMSE when $\Delta\pi$ is small (Table~\ref{tab:main_supp}).
At $K{=}8$ ($n_{\text{expert}}/K{=}31$), coverage remains $\geq$95.6\% but RMSE increases; we recommend $n_{\text{expert}}/K \geq 50$ (Appendix~\ref{app:k8_subgroups}).

\paragraph{CausalForest.}
Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} applies to any estimator whose inputs pass through a confusion matrix; CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal} with a noisy effect modifier $\hat{Z}$ inherits the same $M_{\text{global}}^{-1} M_s$ structure.
With CausalForest ($K{=}4$, extreme, $n{=}500$), EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.191 to 0.039 (4.9$\times$) with coverage 0.90; global amplifies bias up to 5.9$\times$ (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}; bootstrap SE in Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Main results (extreme heterogeneity). Metrics averaged over subgroups, $z$-levels, 100 MC runs. Bold: lowest $|\text{bias}|$. $^\dagger$RMSE exceeds Global. F-L Scalar: $\hat{\tau}/(1{-}2\bar{\pi})$~\cite{frazis2003estimating}; F-L Per-sub.: per-subgroup variant (binary $Z$ only). Moderate/TweetEval in Table~\ref{tab:main_supp}; MC SEs in Appendix~\ref{app:mcse}.}
\label{tab:main_results}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{ll ccc}
\toprule
Configuration & Method & $|\text{Bias}|$ & RMSE & 95\% CI Cov. \\
\midrule
\multirow{6}{*}{\shortstack[l]{DIM\\$K{=}2$, $n{=}250$}}
 & Naive & 0.058 & 0.090 & 0.82 \\
 & Global & 0.059 & 0.099 & 0.87 \\
 & F-L Scalar & 0.122 & 0.159 & 0.68 \\
 & F-L Per-sub. & 0.168 & 0.220 & 0.65 \\
 & Strat.\ MLE & 0.012 & 0.094 & 0.95 \\
 & HB EC-HTE & \textbf{0.008} & 0.089 & 0.94 \\
\midrule
\multirow{4}{*}{\shortstack[l]{DIM\\$K{=}4$, $n{=}500$}}

 & HB EC-HTE & 0.012 & 0.120 & 0.96 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{\shortstack[l]{CausalForest\\$K{=}4$, $n{=}500$}}
 & Naive & 0.208 & 0.231 & 0.44 \\
 & Global & 0.191 & 0.244 & 0.58 \\
 & EC-HTE Forest & \textbf{0.039} & 0.180 & 0.90 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

\subsection{Actionable Diagnostic Without EC-HTE}
\label{sec:diagnostic}

Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} provides a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic: global correction increases bias in subgroup $s$ iff $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$, computable from a pilot sample without estimating treatment effects.
The diagnostic achieves AUC $= 0.63$ across 16 real LLM--dataset combinations; restricting to subgroups with $\Delta\tau > 0$ recovers AUC $= 1.0$ ($0.86$ on synthetic grids; Figure~\ref{fig:roc}, Appendix~\ref{app:screening}).
For $K{=}2$, $|\delta_0|{=}|\delta_1|$ limits discrimination; a meta-criterion ($\max_s \mathrm{score}(s) > 1$) recovers reliability for $K{\geq}4$ (Appendix~\ref{app:screening}).

The condition number $\kappa(\hat{C}_s)$ provides a practical guard: $\kappa > 100$ triggers fallback; all 13 tested LLM--dataset combinations fall in $\kappa \in (1.25, 3]$ with calibrated coverage $\geq$93\% (Appendix~\ref{app:kappa_analysis}).

1	\section{Related Work}
2	\label{sec:related}
3	
4	\paragraph{Measurement error and annotation models.}
5	Classical measurement error theory shows that correction via estimated error models can amplify MSE when the error structure is misspecified~\cite{fuller1987measurement,carroll2006measurement}; Bayesian approaches require informative priors when identification is weak~\cite{gustafson2003measurement}, and nonparametric methods use repeated measurements or instruments to recover the true distribution~\cite{hu2008nonparametric}.
6	
7	Three distinctions separate our contribution from prior measurement error analyses.
8	First, we study effect modifier misclassification---the mismeasured variable defines the CATE function itself---rather than regressor~\cite{frazis2003estimating,carroll2006measurement} or confounder~\cite{ogburn2012nondifferential,greenland1980effect} error, where attenuation is the primary concern.
9	Second, Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} derives a bias identity for correction-induced bias---bias created by the debiasing procedure---rather than bounding the attenuation from misclassification itself.
10	Concretely, \citet{frazis2003estimating} derive scalar attenuation for the uncorrected estimator under homogeneous misclassification; Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} characterizes a structurally distinct quantity---correction-induced bias that is subgroup-specific, potentially sign-reversing, and absent from the uncorrected estimator.
11	The homogeneous-error setting ($K{=}1$, $\delta_s{=}0$) is a degenerate case recovering classical attenuation~\cite{blackwell2017unified}; empirically, F-L correction produces higher bias under heterogeneous misclassification, while EC-HTE achieves near-oracle performance (Appendix~\ref{app:fl_comparison}).
12	Third, the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ product structure arises only under heterogeneous error rates; all homogeneous-error analyses~\cite{battistin2014treatment,fong2021machine} miss this interaction entirely.
13	In the annotation literature, \citet{dawid1979maximum} introduced confusion matrix estimation for multiple annotators, with extensions to item difficulty, annotator competence, and hierarchical priors~\cite{passonneau2014benefits,hovy2013learning,paun2018comparing}.
14	Our hierarchical estimator (Section~\ref{sec:method}) adapts this architecture from label aggregation to causal inference, tying the prior structure to the subgroup dimension that defines treatment effect heterogeneity.
15	
16	\paragraph{HTE estimation and LLM annotation error.}
17	Causal forests~\cite{athey2016recursive,wager2018causal}, double/debiased ML~\cite{chernozhukov2018dml,semenova2021debiased}, doubly-robust CATE estimators~\cite{kennedy2023dr}, and meta-learners~\cite{kunzel2019metalearners} all assume that covariates defining heterogeneity are observed without error; when the effect modifier is misclassified, CATE estimates conflate effects across groups.
18	EC-HTE provides upstream correction that restores valid inputs to any downstream estimator.
19	The corrected pseudo-outcomes are in principle compatible with other HTE estimators such as the R-learner~\citep{nie2021quasi}.
20	For broader perspectives on causal inference with text data, see \citet{feder2022causal} and \citet{keith2020text}; \citet{wang2020methods} study inference correction when outcomes are ML-predicted, a related but distinct problem from effect modifier misclassification.
21	LLMs now match crowd-worker accuracy on many classification tasks~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp,pangakis2023automated}, but \citet{ashwin2025bias} show that error rates vary by up to $5\times$ across demographic subgroups; \citet{cheng2024err} demonstrate that prompt optimization can reduce such error, a complementary preprocessing step.
22	This subgroup-varying error distorts the very contrasts that define the research question; prior work documents the pattern without correcting downstream causal estimands.
23	Concurrent work identifies variance-side LLM measurement error~\cite{messing2026hidden}; \citet{camuffo2025variance} characterize five variance sources in LLM annotation, complementary to our bias-side analysis.
24	Temperature or Platt scaling~\cite{guo2017calibration} reduces per-subgroup $\pi_s$ but does not eliminate heterogeneity $\Delta\pi$; EC-HTE corrects the residual $\delta_s$-driven bias that persists post-calibration (Appendix~\ref{app:calibration} empirically confirms this complementarity).
25	
26	\paragraph{Prediction-powered and design-based correction.}
27	PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,zrnic2024cross} and DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl} correct population-level aggregates assuming homogeneous prediction error.
28	In our setting---binary effect modifier with known subgroup structure, a special case of the broader problems DSL addresses---DSL's measurement error correction reduces, under the confusion-matrix parameterization we adopt, to confusion matrix inversion: pooled DSL is equivalent to our Global baseline, and per-subgroup DSL to Stratified MLE (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}; Appendix~\ref{app:ppi_comparison}).
29	EC-HTE adds hierarchical partial pooling across subgroups, borrowing strength to reduce variance---a mechanism outside the DSL framework.
30	\citet{audinet2025benchmarking} benchmark DSL and PPI debiasing for LLM-based parameter estimation, documenting bias-variance tradeoffs analogous to our findings; their analysis targets population-level parameters rather than subgroup-conditional estimands, leaving the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ interaction we formalize unaddressed.
31	\citet{mozer2026ppi} extend PPI to arm-specific ATE correction; PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} targets conditional estimands but corrects outcome-side error ($\hat{Y}$ given true $Z$), not covariate-side misclassification; ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv} targets the outcome model rather than the heterogeneity structure.
32	None corrects bias when the mismeasured variable is the effect modifier indexing the CATE function.
33	\citet{imai2010causal} study treatment misclassification via instrumental variables or partial identification; \citet{ura2015heterogeneous} extends this to HTE with mismeasured treatment via IV.
34	\citet{miao2018identifying} develop proximal causal inference for unmeasured confounders using proxy variables; our setting differs because $\hat{Z}$ is a moderator proxy rather than a confounder proxy, admitting confusion-matrix correction without the identification constraints of the proximal framework.
35	Extended discussion appears in Appendix~\ref{app:related}.
36	Our validation combines synthetic DGPs, semi-synthetic experiments, and real LLM confusion matrices, consistent with PPI and DSL evaluation methodology; Appendix~\ref{app:multilm} validates both $\Delta\pi$ heterogeneity and the bias identity itself ($R^2 = 0.975$) across 11 model--dataset combinations.

Three distinctions separate our contribution from prior measurement error analyses.
First, we study effect modifier misclassification---the mismeasured variable defines the CATE function itself---rather than regressor~\cite{frazis2003estimating,carroll2006measurement} or confounder~\cite{ogburn2012nondifferential,greenland1980effect} error, where attenuation is the primary concern.
Second, Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} derives a bias identity for correction-induced bias---bias created by the debiasing procedure---rather than bounding the attenuation from misclassification itself.
Concretely, \citet{frazis2003estimating} derive scalar attenuation for the uncorrected estimator under homogeneous misclassification; Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} characterizes a structurally distinct quantity---correction-induced bias that is subgroup-specific, potentially sign-reversing, and absent from the uncorrected estimator.
The homogeneous-error setting ($K{=}1$, $\delta_s{=}0$) is a degenerate case recovering classical attenuation~\cite{blackwell2017unified}; empirically, F-L correction produces higher bias under heterogeneous misclassification, while EC-HTE achieves near-oracle performance (Appendix~\ref{app:fl_comparison}).
Third, the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ product structure arises only under heterogeneous error rates; all homogeneous-error analyses~\cite{battistin2014treatment,fong2021machine} miss this interaction entirely.
In the annotation literature, \citet{dawid1979maximum} introduced confusion matrix estimation for multiple annotators, with extensions to item difficulty, annotator competence, and hierarchical priors~\cite{passonneau2014benefits,hovy2013learning,paun2018comparing}.
Our hierarchical estimator (Section~\ref{sec:method}) adapts this architecture from label aggregation to causal inference, tying the prior structure to the subgroup dimension that defines treatment effect heterogeneity.

\paragraph{HTE estimation and LLM annotation error.}
Causal forests~\cite{athey2016recursive,wager2018causal}, double/debiased ML~\cite{chernozhukov2018dml,semenova2021debiased}, doubly-robust CATE estimators~\cite{kennedy2023dr}, and meta-learners~\cite{kunzel2019metalearners} all assume that covariates defining heterogeneity are observed without error; when the effect modifier is misclassified, CATE estimates conflate effects across groups.
EC-HTE provides upstream correction that restores valid inputs to any downstream estimator.
The corrected pseudo-outcomes are in principle compatible with other HTE estimators such as the R-learner~\citep{nie2021quasi}.
For broader perspectives on causal inference with text data, see \citet{feder2022causal} and \citet{keith2020text}; \citet{wang2020methods} study inference correction when outcomes are ML-predicted, a related but distinct problem from effect modifier misclassification.
LLMs now match crowd-worker accuracy on many classification tasks~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp,pangakis2023automated}, but \citet{ashwin2025bias} show that error rates vary by up to $5\times$ across demographic subgroups; \citet{cheng2024err} demonstrate that prompt optimization can reduce such error, a complementary preprocessing step.
This subgroup-varying error distorts the very contrasts that define the research question; prior work documents the pattern without correcting downstream causal estimands.
Concurrent work identifies variance-side LLM measurement error~\cite{messing2026hidden}; \citet{camuffo2025variance} characterize five variance sources in LLM annotation, complementary to our bias-side analysis.
Temperature or Platt scaling~\cite{guo2017calibration} reduces per-subgroup $\pi_s$ but does not eliminate heterogeneity $\Delta\pi$; EC-HTE corrects the residual $\delta_s$-driven bias that persists post-calibration (Appendix~\ref{app:calibration} empirically confirms this complementarity).

\paragraph{Prediction-powered and design-based correction.}
PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,zrnic2024cross} and DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl} correct population-level aggregates assuming homogeneous prediction error.
In our setting---binary effect modifier with known subgroup structure, a special case of the broader problems DSL addresses---DSL's measurement error correction reduces, under the confusion-matrix parameterization we adopt, to confusion matrix inversion: pooled DSL is equivalent to our Global baseline, and per-subgroup DSL to Stratified MLE (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}; Appendix~\ref{app:ppi_comparison}).
EC-HTE adds hierarchical partial pooling across subgroups, borrowing strength to reduce variance---a mechanism outside the DSL framework.
\citet{audinet2025benchmarking} benchmark DSL and PPI debiasing for LLM-based parameter estimation, documenting bias-variance tradeoffs analogous to our findings; their analysis targets population-level parameters rather than subgroup-conditional estimands, leaving the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ interaction we formalize unaddressed.
\citet{mozer2026ppi} extend PPI to arm-specific ATE correction; PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} targets conditional estimands but corrects outcome-side error ($\hat{Y}$ given true $Z$), not covariate-side misclassification; ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv} targets the outcome model rather than the heterogeneity structure.
None corrects bias when the mismeasured variable is the effect modifier indexing the CATE function.
\citet{imai2010causal} study treatment misclassification via instrumental variables or partial identification; \citet{ura2015heterogeneous} extends this to HTE with mismeasured treatment via IV.
\citet{miao2018identifying} develop proximal causal inference for unmeasured confounders using proxy variables; our setting differs because $\hat{Z}$ is a moderator proxy rather than a confounder proxy, admitting confusion-matrix correction without the identification constraints of the proximal framework.
Extended discussion appears in Appendix~\ref{app:related}.
Our validation combines synthetic DGPs, semi-synthetic experiments, and real LLM confusion matrices, consistent with PPI and DSL evaluation methodology; Appendix~\ref{app:multilm} validates both $\Delta\pi$ heterogeneity and the bias identity itself ($R^2 = 0.975$) across 11 model--dataset combinations.

\section{EC-HTE: Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects}
\label{sec:method}

Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} identifies per-subgroup misclassification deviation as the bias source; the natural correction is per-subgroup confusion matrix inversion.
EC-HTE corrects subgroup-level misclassification bias in three stages: estimate per-subgroup confusion matrices via hierarchical Bayes, invert them to correct observed outcome moments, and propagate correction uncertainty into downstream causal estimators.
The complete procedure is summarized in Algorithm~\ref{alg:echte} (Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).

\subsection{Hierarchical Bayes Confusion Matrix Estimation}

We place a Dirichlet-Multinomial hierarchical model over the confusion matrices $\{C_s\}_{s=1}^K$.
For each subgroup $s$, row $j$ of $C_s$ has a Dirichlet prior centered at the global pooled confusion matrix $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$: $\text{Dir}(\alpha_0 \cdot \hat{C}_{\text{global},j})$, where $\hat{C}_{\text{global},j}$ is the $j$-th row of the pooled CM and $\alpha_0 > 0$ is a shared concentration parameter estimated via empirical Bayes (marginal likelihood maximization).
Large $\alpha_0$ pulls subgroup estimates toward $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$ (global correction), while small $\alpha_0$ allows subgroup-specific rates to dominate (stratified correction).
This partial pooling---a form of James-Stein shrinkage well-established in small-area estimation---borrows strength across subgroups when estimating confusion matrices from limited expert labels, reducing variance for small subgroups while preserving heterogeneity where data support it.

Posterior inference uses centered empirical Bayes optimization ($<$5ms for $K{=}4$, $N{=}5{,}000$); a full Gibbs MCMC alternative requires $\sim$5s (convergence diagnostics in Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).
Bootstrap SE ($B{=}100$) adds $\sim$0.4s.
HB estimation outperforms stratified MLE in 87.5\% of configurations (21 of 24) across the experimental grid (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}), with the largest gains when $n_{\text{expert}} / K < 100$.
The advantage requires $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ per subgroup; below this threshold, stratified MLE is preferred because the hierarchical model lacks sufficient observations for stable shrinkage.
At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1000$, HB and stratified MLE converge to within 0.5\% on all metrics.
Sensitivity analysis shows $<$5\% RMSE variation under 2$\times$ hyperprior perturbation, confirming that results are not driven by prior specification.

\subsection{Subgroup-Stratified Correction}

Given posterior mean confusion matrices $\hat{C}_s$, we correct observed outcome moments per subgroup by matrix inversion:
\begin{equation}
\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = \hat{C}_s^{-1} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s,
\end{equation}
where $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = [\hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(0, s),\, \hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(1, s)]^\top$ collects the observed conditional outcome moments in subgroup $s$.
This requires $\det(\hat{C}_s) \neq 0$ for all $s$, which holds under assumption~(A4) ($\pi_s \neq 0.5$) but may fail in finite samples when error rates approach degeneracy.
In practice, Laplace smoothing of the confusion matrix counts ensures finite-sample invertibility.
We impose a singularity guard: if the condition number $\kappa(\hat{C}_s) > 100$ (for a $2{\times}2$ symmetric confusion matrix, this corresponds to $\pi_s > 0.495$, i.e., near-random classification), subgroup $s$ falls back to global correction $\bar{C}^{-1}$; when the fallback triggers, the standard error computation also uses $\bar{C}^{-1}$ for that subgroup, ensuring consistency between point estimates and confidence intervals.
This hard guard prevents numerical catastrophe; $\kappa \leq 1.25$ is a sufficient condition for strongest bias reduction (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}), though EC-HTE maintains calibrated coverage ($\geq$93\%) across the wider $\kappa \in [1.4, 3.0]$ range observed in practice (Appendix~\ref{app:kappa_analysis}).

The contrast with global correction is direct.
Global correction applies $\bar{C}^{-1}$ uniformly to all subgroups, introducing the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ bias identified in Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}.
Subgroup-stratified correction eliminates this bias by matching each subgroup's correction to its own misclassification structure, at the cost of higher variance from estimating $K$ separate confusion matrices (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}).

\subsection{Variance-Adjusted CausalForest}

For heterogeneous treatment effect estimation, we feed corrected covariates into CausalForestDML~\cite{wager2018causal} with honest splitting.
The forest produces per-observation standard error estimates $\text{se}_i$.
To account for confusion matrix correction, we propagate uncertainty through the inverse mapping:
\begin{equation}
\text{se}_{\text{corrected},i} = \sqrt{\text{diag}\!\left(\hat{C}_{S_i}^{-1}\, \text{diag}(\text{se}_i^2)\, \hat{C}_{S_i}^{-\top}\right)}.
\end{equation}
This plug-in SE conditions on $\hat{C}_s$, neglecting CM estimation uncertainty; at $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 100$ this is negligible, but below this threshold a full bootstrap ($B{=}100$; re-estimate CM and re-fit per replicate) maintains $\geq$95\% coverage across all budgets tested ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{25, 50, 75, 100, 200\}$); even plug-in SE achieves $\geq$91\% at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}25$ (Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}).
When $n_{\text{expert}}/K < 50$, we recommend bootstrap SE; otherwise plug-in SE suffices.

\paragraph{Diagnostic criterion.}
Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} provides a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic: global correction harms subgroup $s$ if and only if $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$, a condition depending only on per-subgroup misclassification rates estimable from a pilot sample.
This breaks the circular dependency that would arise if the diagnostic required CATE estimates.
A threshold classifier achieves AUC~=~0.86 at the subgroup level, reaching 1.0 when restricted to subgroups with $\tau_s > 0$ (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).

\paragraph{Composition with PPCI.}
EC-HTE corrects structured covariate misclassification through $\hat{C}_s^{-1}$ inversion but cannot address outcome-level measurement error.
PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} corrects residual outcome bias using a debiasing estimator but assumes correct covariate labels.
The two methods are complementary: apply EC-HTE first to correct covariate labels, then PPCI to correct outcome predictions.
Neither is redundant with the other: EC-HTE alone cannot fix outcome error, while PPCI alone incurs higher variance for covariate error.
Under both error types simultaneously, the composition reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007 (Appendix~\ref{sec:ppci}).

\section{Experiments}

\subsection{Setup}

We test on synthetic ($N{=}5{,}000$, $K \in \{2, 4\}$, controlled $\Delta\tau$ and $\Delta\pi$, 100 MC runs) and semi-synthetic (TweetEval sentiment~\cite{barbieri2020tweeteval}, $K{=}4$ unbalanced subgroups, $\pi \in \{0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25\}$) DGPs; full specifications in Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}.

We compare: (1) \textit{Naive} (no correction), (2) \textit{Global} (pooled confusion matrix, equivalent to PPI/DSL~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,egami2024dsl} with homogeneous error), (3) \textit{Stratified MLE} (per-subgroup DSL without shrinkage), (4) \textit{HB EC-HTE} (our method), (5) \textit{PPCI}~\cite{sui2026ppci}, and (6) \textit{EC-HTE+PPCI}.
For CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal}, we compare naive, global, and EC-HTE variants.
Primary metrics are $|\text{bias}|$, RMSE, and 95\% CI coverage, averaged across subgroups and 100 MC runs.
Robustness validation covers hate speech, six OpenAI models, subgroup misspecification, asymmetric confusion matrices, confounded treatment, outcome-dependent misclassification (all $\geq$93.5\% coverage), and treatment-dependent misclassification ($\approx$90\% at $\gamma_T \leq 0.05$; Appendices~\ref{app:hatespeech}--\ref{app:treatment_dep}).

\subsection{Empirical Validation of the Bias Identity}
\label{sec:bias_mechanism}

We verify Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} on a $K{=}2$ grid (520 configurations, $\Delta\pi \in [0, 0.25]$, $\Delta\tau \in (0, 0.50]$) and a $K{=}4$ grid (Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}).
Regressing observed subgroup bias on $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1{-}2\bar{\pi})$ yields $R^2 = 0.994$ ($K{=}2$) and $0.974$ ($K{=}4$); residual variance reflects MC noise ($R^2 \geq 0.976$ even at $P(Z{=}1) = 0.1$; Appendix~\ref{app:classimbalance}).
Global correction worsens bias in 50\% of $K{=}2$ configurations (260/520, excluding $\Delta\pi{=}0$), with amplification reaching 2.86$\times$ ($K{=}2$) and 2.41$\times$ ($K{=}4$); Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} visualizes the amplification surface.
Beyond amplification, global correction reverses the sign of estimated CATE---concluding a protective treatment is harmful---in 14.9\% of configurations at $\tau(0) = 0.03$ (31\% at $\tau(0) = 0.01$; critical threshold $\tau(0) < 0.089$, matching Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}), with all eight real LLMs amplifying bias under global correction; EC-HTE eliminates sign reversal entirely (Figure~\ref{fig:sign_reversal}; Appendix~\ref{app:policy_reversal}).

\subsection{EC-HTE Evaluation}
\label{sec:ec_hte_eval}

Table~\ref{tab:main_results} presents the main results across representative configurations.
In the $K{=}2$ extreme row, global correction \emph{increases} $|\text{bias}|$ relative to naive (0.059 vs.\ 0.058), confirming the over-correction mechanism of Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}.
F-L scalar correction increases $|\text{bias}|$ to 0.122 (coverage 0.68); F-L per-subgroup to 0.168 as $(1{-}2\pi_s) \to 0$---both worse than naive (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}).
HB EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.008 (7.4$\times$) at $K{=}2$ and from 0.056 to 0.012 (4.7$\times$) at $K{=}4$, maintaining near-nominal coverage (0.94--0.96) with lower RMSE than stratified MLE.
Under moderate heterogeneity and in TweetEval ($K{=}4$), methods converge ($p > 0.05$); EC-HTE incurs higher RMSE when $\Delta\pi$ is small (Table~\ref{tab:main_supp}).
At $K{=}8$ ($n_{\text{expert}}/K{=}31$), coverage remains $\geq$95.6\% but RMSE increases; we recommend $n_{\text{expert}}/K \geq 50$ (Appendix~\ref{app:k8_subgroups}).

\paragraph{CausalForest.}
Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} applies to any estimator whose inputs pass through a confusion matrix; CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal} with a noisy effect modifier $\hat{Z}$ inherits the same $M_{\text{global}}^{-1} M_s$ structure.
With CausalForest ($K{=}4$, extreme, $n{=}500$), EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.191 to 0.039 (4.9$\times$) with coverage 0.90; global amplifies bias up to 5.9$\times$ (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}; bootstrap SE in Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}).

\begin{table}[t]

\subsection{Actionable Diagnostic Without EC-HTE}
\label{sec:diagnostic}

Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} provides a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic: global correction increases bias in subgroup $s$ iff $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$, computable from a pilot sample without estimating treatment effects.
The diagnostic achieves AUC $= 0.63$ across 16 real LLM--dataset combinations; restricting to subgroups with $\Delta\tau > 0$ recovers AUC $= 1.0$ ($0.86$ on synthetic grids; Figure~\ref{fig:roc}, Appendix~\ref{app:screening}).
For $K{=}2$, $|\delta_0|{=}|\delta_1|$ limits discrimination; a meta-criterion ($\max_s \mathrm{score}(s) > 1$) recovers reliability for $K{\geq}4$ (Appendix~\ref{app:screening}).

The condition number $\kappa(\hat{C}_s)$ provides a practical guard: $\kappa > 100$ triggers fallback; all 13 tested LLM--dataset combinations fall in $\kappa \in (1.25, 3]$ with calibrated coverage $\geq$93\% (Appendix~\ref{app:kappa_analysis}).
Budget crossover, $K{=}8$ scalability, and multi-LLM validation ($R^2 = 0.975$) appear in Appendices~\ref{sec:budget}--\ref{app:multilm}.

Primary metrics are $|\text{bias}|$, RMSE, and 95\% CI coverage, averaged across subgroups and 100 MC runs.

\subsection{Empirical Validation of the Bias Identity}
\label{sec:bias_mechanism}

We verify Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} on a $K{=}2$ grid (520 configurations, $\Delta\pi \in [0, 0.25]$, $\Delta\tau \in (0, 0.50]$) and a $K{=}4$ grid (Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}).
Regressing observed subgroup bias on $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1{-}2\bar{\pi})$ yields $R^2 = 0.994$ ($K{=}2$) and $0.974$ ($K{=}4$); residual variance reflects MC noise ($R^2 \geq 0.976$ even at $P(Z{=}1) = 0.1$; Appendix~\ref{app:classimbalance}).

\label{sec:ec_hte_eval}

Table~\ref{tab:main_results} presents the main results across representative configurations.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Measurement error and annotation models.}
Classical measurement error theory shows that correction via estimated error models can amplify MSE when the error structure is misspecified~\cite{fuller1987measurement,carroll2006measurement}; Bayesian approaches require informative priors when identification is weak~\cite{gustafson2003measurement}, and nonparametric methods use repeated measurements or instruments to recover the true distribution~\cite{hu2008nonparametric}.

Three distinctions separate our contribution from prior measurement error analyses.
First, we study effect modifier misclassification---the mismeasured variable defines the CATE function itself---rather than regressor~\cite{frazis2003estimating,carroll2006measurement} or confounder~\cite{ogburn2012nondifferential,greenland1980effect} error, where attenuation is the primary concern.
Second, Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} derives a bias identity for correction-induced bias---bias created by the debiasing procedure---rather than bounding the attenuation from misclassification itself.
Concretely, \citet{frazis2003estimating} derive scalar attenuation for the uncorrected estimator under homogeneous misclassification; Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} characterizes a structurally distinct quantity---correction-induced bias that is subgroup-specific, potentially sign-reversing, and absent from the uncorrected estimator.
The homogeneous-error setting ($K{=}1$, $\delta_s{=}0$) is a degenerate case recovering classical attenuation~\cite{blackwell2017unified}; empirically, F-L correction produces higher bias under heterogeneous misclassification, while EC-HTE achieves near-oracle performance (Appendix~\ref{app:fl_comparison}).
Third, the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ product structure arises only under heterogeneous error rates; all homogeneous-error analyses~\cite{battistin2014treatment,fong2021machine} miss this interaction entirely.
In the annotation literature, \citet{dawid1979maximum} introduced confusion matrix estimation for multiple annotators, with extensions to item difficulty, annotator competence, and hierarchical priors~\cite{passonneau2014benefits,hovy2013learning,paun2018comparing}.
Our hierarchical estimator (Section~\ref{sec:method}) adapts this architecture from label aggregation to causal inference, tying the prior structure to the subgroup dimension that defines treatment effect heterogeneity.

\paragraph{HTE estimation and LLM annotation error.}
Causal forests~\cite{athey2016recursive,wager2018causal}, double/debiased ML~\cite{chernozhukov2018dml,semenova2021debiased}, doubly-robust CATE estimators~\cite{kennedy2023dr}, and meta-learners~\cite{kunzel2019metalearners} all assume that covariates defining heterogeneity are observed without error; when the effect modifier is misclassified, CATE estimates conflate effects across groups.
EC-HTE provides upstream correction that restores valid inputs to any downstream estimator.
The corrected pseudo-outcomes are in principle compatible with other HTE estimators such as the R-learner~\citep{nie2021quasi}.
For broader perspectives on causal inference with text data, see \citet{feder2022causal} and \citet{keith2020text}; \citet{wang2020methods} study inference correction when outcomes are ML-predicted, a related but distinct problem from effect modifier misclassification.
LLMs now match crowd-worker accuracy on many classification tasks~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp,pangakis2023automated}, but \citet{ashwin2025bias} show that error rates vary by up to $5\times$ across demographic subgroups; \citet{cheng2024err} demonstrate that prompt optimization can reduce such error, a complementary preprocessing step.
This subgroup-varying error distorts the very contrasts that define the research question; prior work documents the pattern without correcting downstream causal estimands.
Concurrent work identifies variance-side LLM measurement error~\cite{messing2026hidden}; \citet{camuffo2025variance} characterize five variance sources in LLM annotation, complementary to our bias-side analysis.
Temperature or Platt scaling~\cite{guo2017calibration} reduces per-subgroup $\pi_s$ but does not eliminate heterogeneity $\Delta\pi$; EC-HTE corrects the residual $\delta_s$-driven bias that persists post-calibration (Appendix~\ref{app:calibration} empirically confirms this complementarity).

\paragraph{Prediction-powered and design-based correction.}
PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,zrnic2024cross} and DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl} correct population-level aggregates assuming homogeneous prediction error.
In our setting---binary effect modifier with known subgroup structure, a special case of the broader problems DSL addresses---DSL's measurement error correction reduces, under the confusion-matrix parameterization we adopt, to confusion matrix inversion: pooled DSL is equivalent to our Global baseline, and per-subgroup DSL to Stratified MLE (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}; Appendix~\ref{app:ppi_comparison}).
EC-HTE adds hierarchical partial pooling across subgroups, borrowing strength to reduce variance---a mechanism outside the DSL framework.
\citet{audinet2025benchmarking} benchmark DSL and PPI debiasing for LLM-based parameter estimation, documenting bias-variance tradeoffs analogous to our findings; their analysis targets population-level parameters rather than subgroup-conditional estimands, leaving the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ interaction we formalize unaddressed.
\citet{mozer2026ppi} extend PPI to arm-specific ATE correction; PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} targets conditional estimands but corrects outcome-side error ($\hat{Y}$ given true $Z$), not covariate-side misclassification; ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv} targets the outcome model rather than the heterogeneity structure.
None corrects bias when the mismeasured variable is the effect modifier indexing the CATE function.
\citet{imai2010causal} study treatment misclassification via instrumental variables or partial identification; \citet{ura2015heterogeneous} extends this to HTE with mismeasured treatment via IV.
\citet{miao2018identifying} develop proximal causal inference for unmeasured confounders using proxy variables; our setting differs because $\hat{Z}$ is a moderator proxy rather than a confounder proxy, admitting confusion-matrix correction without the identification constraints of the proximal framework.
Extended discussion appears in Appendix~\ref{app:related}.
Our validation combines synthetic DGPs, semi-synthetic experiments, and real LLM confusion matrices, consistent with PPI and DSL evaluation methodology; Appendix~\ref{app:multilm} validates both $\Delta\pi$ heterogeneity and the bias identity itself ($R^2 = 0.975$) across 11 model--dataset combinations.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Measurement error and annotation models.}
Classical measurement error theory shows that correction via estimated error models can amplify MSE when the error structure is misspecified~\cite{fuller1987measurement,carroll2006measurement}; Bayesian approaches require informative priors when identification is weak~\cite{gustafson2003measurement}, and nonparametric methods use repeated measurements or instruments to recover the true distribution~\cite{hu2008nonparametric}.

Three distinctions separate our contribution from prior measurement error analyses.
First, we study effect modifier misclassification---the mismeasured variable defines the CATE function itself---rather than regressor~\cite{frazis2003estimating,carroll2006measurement} or confounder~\cite{ogburn2012nondifferential,greenland1980effect} error, where attenuation is the primary concern.
Second, Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} derives a bias identity for correction-induced bias---bias created by the debiasing procedure---rather than bounding the attenuation from misclassification itself.

The homogeneous-error setting ($K{=}1$, $\delta_s{=}0$) is a degenerate case recovering classical attenuation~\cite{blackwell2017unified}; empirically, F-L correction produces higher bias under heterogeneous misclassification, while EC-HTE achieves near-oracle performance (Appendix~\ref{app:fl_comparison}).
Third, the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ product structure arises only under heterogeneous error rates; all homogeneous-error analyses~\cite{battistin2014treatment,fong2021machine} miss this interaction entirely.
In the annotation literature, \citet{dawid1979maximum} introduced confusion matrix estimation for multiple annotators, with extensions to item difficulty, annotator competence, and hierarchical priors~\cite{passonneau2014benefits,hovy2013learning,paun2018comparing}.
Our hierarchical estimator (Section~\ref{sec:method}) adapts this architecture from label aggregation to causal inference, tying the prior structure to the subgroup dimension that defines treatment effect heterogeneity.

\paragraph{Prediction-powered and design-based correction.}

\section{Experiments}

\subsection{Setup}

We test on synthetic ($N{=}5{,}000$, $K \in \{2, 4\}$, controlled $\Delta\tau$ and $\Delta\pi$, 100 MC runs) and semi-synthetic (TweetEval sentiment~\cite{barbieri2020tweeteval}, $K{=}4$ unbalanced subgroups, $\pi \in \{0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25\}$) DGPs; full specifications in Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}.

We compare: (1) \textit{Naive} (no correction), (2) \textit{Global} (pooled confusion matrix, equivalent to PPI/DSL~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,egami2024dsl} with homogeneous error), (3) \textit{Stratified MLE} (per-subgroup DSL without shrinkage), (4) \textit{HB EC-HTE} (per-subgroup correction), (5) \textit{PPCI}~\cite{sui2026ppci}, and (6) \textit{EC-HTE+PPCI}.
For CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal}, we compare naive, global, and EC-HTE variants.
Primary metrics are $|\text{bias}|$, RMSE, and 95\% CI coverage, averaged across subgroups and 100 MC runs.
Robustness validation covers hate speech, six OpenAI models, subgroup misspecification, asymmetric confusion matrices, confounded treatment, outcome-dependent misclassification (all $\geq$93.5\% coverage), and treatment-dependent misclassification ($\approx$90\% at $\gamma_T \leq 0.05$; Appendices~\ref{app:hatespeech}--\ref{app:treatment_dep}).

\subsection{Empirical Validation of the Bias Identity}
\label{sec:bias_mechanism}

We verify Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} on a $K{=}2$ grid (520 configurations, $\Delta\pi \in [0, 0.25]$, $\Delta\tau \in (0, 0.50]$) and a $K{=}4$ grid (Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}).
Regressing observed subgroup bias on $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1{-}2\bar{\pi})$ yields $R^2 = 0.994$ ($K{=}2$) and $0.974$ ($K{=}4$); residual variance reflects MC noise ($R^2 \geq 0.976$ even at $P(Z{=}1) = 0.1$; Appendix~\ref{app:classimbalance}).
Global correction worsens bias in 50\% of $K{=}2$ configurations (260/520, excluding $\Delta\pi{=}0$), with amplification reaching 2.86$\times$ ($K{=}2$) and 2.41$\times$ ($K{=}4$); Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} visualizes the amplification surface.
Beyond amplification, global correction reverses the sign of estimated CATE---concluding a protective treatment is harmful---in 14.9\% of configurations at $\tau(0) = 0.03$ (31\% at $\tau(0) = 0.01$; critical threshold $\tau(0) < 0.089$, matching Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}), with all eight real LLMs amplifying bias under global correction; EC-HTE eliminates sign reversal entirely (Figure~\ref{fig:sign_reversal}; Appendix~\ref{app:policy_reversal}).

\subsection{Correction Evaluation}
\label{sec:ec_hte_eval}

Table~\ref{tab:main_results} presents the main results across representative configurations.
In the $K{=}2$ extreme row, global correction \emph{increases} $|\text{bias}|$ relative to naive (0.059 vs.\ 0.058), confirming the over-correction mechanism of Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}.
F-L scalar correction increases $|\text{bias}|$ to 0.122 (coverage 0.68); F-L per-subgroup to 0.168 as $(1{-}2\pi_s) \to 0$---both worse than naive (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}).
HB EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.008 (7.4$\times$) at $K{=}2$ and from 0.056 to 0.012 (4.7$\times$) at $K{=}4$, maintaining near-nominal coverage (0.94--0.96) with lower RMSE than stratified MLE.
Under moderate heterogeneity and in TweetEval ($K{=}4$), methods converge ($p > 0.05$); EC-HTE incurs higher RMSE when $\Delta\pi$ is small (Table~\ref{tab:main_supp}).
At $K{=}8$ ($n_{\text{expert}}/K{=}31$), coverage remains $\geq$95.6\% but RMSE increases; we recommend $n_{\text{expert}}/K \geq 50$ (Appendix~\ref{app:k8_subgroups}).

\paragraph{CausalForest.}
Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} applies to any estimator whose inputs pass through a confusion matrix; CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal} with a noisy effect modifier $\hat{Z}$ inherits the same $M_{\text{global}}^{-1} M_s$ structure.
With CausalForest ($K{=}4$, extreme, $n{=}500$), EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.191 to 0.039 (4.9$\times$) with coverage 0.90; global amplifies bias up to 5.9$\times$ (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}; bootstrap SE in Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Main results (extreme heterogeneity). Metrics averaged over subgroups, $z$-levels, 100 MC runs. Bold: lowest $|\text{bias}|$. $^\dagger$RMSE exceeds Global. F-L Scalar: $\hat{\tau}/(1{-}2\bar{\pi})$~\cite{frazis2003estimating}; F-L Per-sub.: per-subgroup variant (binary $Z$ only). Moderate/TweetEval in Table~\ref{tab:main_supp}; MC SEs in Appendix~\ref{app:mcse}.}
\label{tab:main_results}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{ll ccc}
\toprule
Configuration & Method & $|\text{Bias}|$ & RMSE & 95\% CI Cov. \\
\midrule

 & F-L Scalar & 0.122 & 0.159 & 0.68 \\
 & F-L Per-sub. & 0.168 & 0.220 & 0.65 \\
